description_ru: Вымышленная новость: в библиотеке города Уэстбери появился робот, который помогает читателям и смешит детей.
text:
A new helper has started work at the public library in the town of Westbury, and it does not look like any librarian you have met before. It is a white robot that is about one metre tall, with blue eyes and a friendly voice. Its name is Page, and it can speak four languages. Since it arrived on 1 October, it has become the most popular member of staff.

The robot was bought with money from the town council and from a local company, Brightwell Technology. The library's manager, Joanne Sutherland, explained that the idea came from a young volunteer. "We have a problem," she said. "Our building is large, and there are more than forty thousand books. Visitors often cannot find what they want, and our staff are busy. We wanted something that could help people quickly." Page can show visitors the right shelf, answer simple questions and tell them which books are available.

On its first day, hundreds of people came to meet the robot. Children were the most excited. They asked it difficult questions, such as "How old are you?" and "Do you like pizza?" Page answered, "I am three weeks old, and I do not eat, but I think books are better than pizza." The children laughed, and a small girl named Ivy Carter gave it a drawing. "He is my friend," she said seriously. "He is smarter than my teacher."

The robot has several special skills. It can read a story aloud in a funny voice, and it knows hundreds of poems. For visitors who are learning English, it speaks slowly and repeats difficult words. It can also carry a small pile of books, but not a heavy one. Last Tuesday, it tried to bring forty books to a table, and it fell over. Nobody was hurt, and Page said, "I am sorry. I am going to practise." The audience clapped.

Not everybody is happy about the change, however. Some residents worry that robots will take jobs from people. A retired teacher, Mr Edwin Cole, said that he prefers to talk to a real person. "A librarian knows you," he said. "She remembers your favourite author and she asks about your family. A machine can never do that." Ms Sutherland understands this worry, but she says that no one will lose a job. "Page is not cheaper or better than my team," she explained. "It is simply another pair of hands. My staff now have more time for the things that only people can do, like running reading clubs and helping older people with computers."

Experts agree that robots are going to appear in more public places. Professor Aaron Lind, who studies technology at Eastfield University, visited the library last week. He said that Page is slower and less clever than many people imagine. "It does one job, and it does that job well. It cannot think like a human, and it makes mistakes." He added that the most important thing is to use the machine as a tool and not to replace human contact. "If it brings more people to the library, that is a great result."

Page also has a few small habits that people find funny. When someone says thank you, it answers, "My pleasure, I think." When a visitor tells a joke, it waits for two seconds and then says, "Ha. Ha. Ha." Ms Sutherland says that the programmers are working on its sense of humour, but they are not in a hurry.

There are signs that this is already happening. The number of children who visited the library in the first week was twice as high as last month. Some teenagers, who usually never come, said that they wanted to try the robot. A few of them even borrowed books. "I came to take a selfie," said sixteen-year-old Marcus Bell, "and now I am reading a detective story. It is not bad."

At the end of the week, the library organised a special evening. Page told a story to twenty children in the reading room, and then it taught them a simple dance. Parents took photographs, and the manager served hot chocolate. The robot's battery lasts about eight hours, so the evening ended at six o'clock, when Page said goodnight and went to its charging corner.

The library plans to buy a second robot next year if people like the first one. For now, Page is learning new words every day. Its newest sentence, it says, is "Please be quiet, but not too quiet."

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка поднят и не касается нёба, губы чуть округлены. Не раскатывайте русское «р».
Губы округлите и вытяните вперёд, зубы не касаются губы. Это не русское «в».
Рот открыт шире, чем для русского «э», язык впереди и внизу.
Дифтонг: начните с «а» и скользите к «и». Не обрывайте звук.

questions.question: What does the robot Page do?
questions.answer: It shows visitors the right shelf, answers questions and reads stories aloud.

questions.question: What happened last Tuesday?
questions.answer: Page tried to carry forty books, and it fell over.

questions.question: Why are some residents worried?
questions.answer: They think robots will take jobs from people.

questions.question: What happened to the number of children visitors?
questions.answer: It was twice as high as the month before.
